questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The Constitution of India was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on:
questions.explanation: The Constituent Assembly formally adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949 — a date now observed as Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas). 15 August 1947 is Independence Day, not the adoption of the Constitution. 26 January 1950 is the date the Constitution came into FORCE (Republic Day), not the date of adoption. 9 December 1946 is the first meeting date of the Constituent Assembly, not the adoption date.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the Preamble of the Indian Constitution:

(i) The Preamble declares India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic.
(ii) The words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment, 1976.
(iii) The Preamble is enforceable in a court of law.
(iv) The Preamble is regarded as the 'soul' or 'identity card' of the Constitution.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — the Preamble as amended declares India as Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic. (ii) is correct — 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976). (iv) is correct — the Preamble is famously described as the 'soul' of the Constitution (K.M. Munshi called it the 'political horoscope'). (iii) is INCORRECT — the Preamble itself is NOT enforceable in a court; it serves as an interpretive guide but cannot be sued upon. Any option including (iii) is therefore wrong.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution are contained in:
questions.explanation: Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Constitution, spanning Articles 12 to 35. Part II (Articles 5-11) deals with Citizenship. Part IV (Articles 36-51) contains the Directive Principles of State Policy — non-justiciable guidelines. Part V (Articles 52-151) relates to the Union Government (President, Parliament, judiciary etc.).

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The Directive Principles of State Policy are not enforceable in a court of law.
Reason (R): Article 37 of the Constitution declares the Directive Principles as non-justiciable but fundamental in the governance of the country.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: (A) is correct — Directive Principles cannot be enforced by any court. (R) is correct — Article 37 explicitly states DPSPs are 'not enforceable by any court' but 'fundamental in the governance of the country'. (R) directly explains (A) — the non-enforceability is precisely what Article 37 declares. Option 2 wrongly denies the explanatory link. Options 3 and 4 wrongly deny (A) or (R).

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText:
Match the following Articles of the Constitution with their subject matter:

Column I:
(a) Article 14
(b) Article 19
(c) Article 21
(d) Article 32

Column II:
(i) Right to constitutional remedies (writs)
(ii) Right to equality before law
(iii) Right to life and personal liberty
(iv) Six freedoms (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession)

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: Article 14 = equality before law → (a)-(ii). Article 19 = six freedoms (speech, assembly, etc.) → (b)-(iv). Article 21 = life and personal liberty → (c)-(iii). Article 32 = right to constitutional remedies (Dr. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution) → (d)-(i). The distractor (a)-(iv) confuses equality with the six freedoms. (a)-(iii) confuses equality with life/liberty. (a)-(i) treats Article 14 as writs.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The number of Fundamental Duties currently listed under Article 51A of the Constitution is:
questions.explanation: Originally 10 Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). An 11th duty (providing education to children between 6 and 14 years by parents/guardians) was added by the 86th Amendment (2002). So the current number is 11. '10' was the original count before 2002. '12' and '9' are simply incorrect.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of India is appointed by the:
questions.explanation: Under Article 124(2), the Chief Justice of India is appointed by the President of India, after consultation with judges of the SC and HCs (as further evolved by the Second and Third Judges cases into the Collegium system). The Prime Minister does not appoint judges — the PM is part of the executive advice but the formal appointment is by the President. Parliament does not appoint judges but can remove them via impeachment. The Chief Election Commissioner is himself/herself appointed by the President and has no role in judicial appointments.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText:
Which of the following are 'writs' that can be issued by the Supreme Court under Article 32 and by High Courts under Article 226?

(i) Habeas Corpus
(ii) Mandamus
(iii) Certiorari
(iv) Impeachment

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: The five constitutional writs are Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Certiorari, Prohibition and Quo Warranto — so (i), (ii) and (iii) are all valid writs. (iv) 'Impeachment' is NOT a writ — it is a parliamentary process for removing certain constitutional office holders (President, judges, etc.). Any option including (iv) is therefore wrong.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The __________ is the head of the state government in an Indian state.
options: Chief Justice of the High Court
questions.explanation: The Governor is the constitutional head of a state, similar to the President at the Union level — appointed by the President under Article 155. The Chief Minister is the head of the state government (i.e., the political/executive head who commands the majority in the Assembly), but the question asks about the head of the STATE, which is the constitutional/nominal head (Governor). The Chief Justice of the HC heads the state judiciary. The Speaker presides over the Legislative Assembly but is not the head of the state.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The Rajya Sabha (Council of States) has a maximum strength of:
questions.explanation: The Constitution (Article 80) provides for a maximum strength of 250 members in the Rajya Sabha — 238 representatives of states/UTs elected indirectly plus 12 nominated by the President. '245' is the CURRENT actual strength (not the maximum). '550' and '552' relate to the Lok Sabha (whose maximum was 552 before the 104th amendment; currently effective 543 elected + earlier 2 Anglo-Indian nominations, since discontinued).

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the Parliament of India:

(i) It consists of the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
(ii) Members of the Lok Sabha are directly elected by the people.
(iii) The Rajya Sabha can be dissolved every 5 years.
(iv) A Money Bill can originate only in the Lok Sabha.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — Parliament comprises President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha (Article 79). (ii) is correct — Lok Sabha members are directly elected by universal adult franchise. (iv) is correct — Money Bills can originate ONLY in the Lok Sabha (Article 109). (iii) is INCORRECT — the Rajya Sabha is a PERMANENT house that cannot be dissolved; one-third of its members retire every 2 years. Any option including (iii) is therefore wrong.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The word 'Federal' does not appear in the Indian Constitution; instead, the Constitution describes India as a __________ of States.
questions.explanation: Article 1 of the Constitution declares 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States'. Dr. Ambedkar explained that 'Union' was preferred over 'Federation' to emphasize that Indian states cannot secede — the Union is indestructible. 'Federation' is deliberately not used. 'Confederation' implies a much looser association (states retain sovereignty), which is not India's model. 'Republic' refers to the elected nature of the head of state, not to the structure of the states.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The Election Commission of India was established under which Article of the Constitution?
questions.explanation: Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission of India. Article 148 relates to the Comptroller and Auditor General. Article 148A does not exist. Article 315 deals with the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and State PSCs.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The right to property is no longer a Fundamental Right in India.
Reason (R): The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) removed the right to property from Part III and inserted it as a legal/constitutional right under Article 300A.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: (A) is correct — the right to property is no longer a Fundamental Right. (R) is correct — the 44th Amendment (1978) removed the erstwhile Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 from Part III and placed the right to property in Article 300A as an ordinary constitutional right. (R) directly explains (A). Option 2 wrongly denies the causal link. Options 3 and 4 wrongly deny (A) or (R).

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The Directive Principles of State Policy in the Indian Constitution are borrowed from the constitution of:
questions.explanation: The Directive Principles of State Policy were borrowed from the Irish Constitution (which in turn had drawn from Spanish sources). UK inspired parliamentary democracy and the office of speaker. USA inspired Fundamental Rights, judicial review, and the office of Vice-President. Canada inspired the federal structure with a strong Centre and the term 'Union of States'.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText:
Match the following provisions with the constitution/country from which they were BORROWED:

Column I:
(a) Parliamentary form of government
(b) Fundamental Rights and Judicial Review
(c) Federal structure with a strong Centre
(d) Directive Principles of State Policy

Column II:
(i) Ireland
(ii) United Kingdom
(iii) United States of America
(iv) Canada

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: Parliamentary system → borrowed from UK → (a)-(ii). Fundamental Rights & Judicial Review → USA → (b)-(iii). Federal structure with strong Centre → Canada → (c)-(iv). DPSPs → Ireland → (d)-(i). The distractor (a)-(iii) confuses parliamentary UK with US. (a)-(iv) links parliamentary to Canada — wrong. (a)-(i) links parliamentary to Ireland — wrong.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The Panchayati Raj system was given constitutional status by the:
questions.explanation: The 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 added Part IX (Articles 243 to 243-O) to the Constitution, giving Panchayati Raj Institutions constitutional status. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Fundamental Duties and modified the Preamble; not related to Panchayats. The 44th (1978) removed the Right to Property. The 74th (1992) is a related amendment that gave constitutional status to URBAN local bodies (Nagar Panchayats, Municipalities) — Part IXA.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The maximum tenure of the Lok Sabha under normal circumstances is:
questions.explanation: The Lok Sabha has a normal tenure of 5 years from the date of its first meeting after general elections, after which it stands dissolved automatically (Article 83(2)). During a Proclamation of Emergency, the term can be extended by Parliament by law for a period not exceeding one year at a time. '4 years' is the US House of Representatives model, not India. '6 years' is the Rajya Sabha member's term, not Lok Sabha. '7 years' has no basis.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The concept of a 'Single Citizenship' for the whole of India is borrowed from:
questions.explanation: India adopts SINGLE citizenship on the UK model — an Indian is a citizen of India, not separately of a state. The USA has DUAL citizenship (federal and state). Australia adopts a variation of federalism, not the source of single citizenship. Germany also has state citizenship in addition to federal citizenship in some interpretations, again not India's model source.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText:
Which of the following are considered 'Money Bills' under the Indian Constitution?

(i) Bills imposing a tax.
(ii) Bills regulating the borrowing of money by the Government.
(iii) Bills declaring an emergency.
(iv) Bills involving the withdrawal of money from the Consolidated Fund of India.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: Under Article 110, Money Bills relate to (i) imposition/abolition/alteration of any tax, (ii) borrowing of money by the Government, (iv) custody or issue of money from the Consolidated Fund of India, plus related matters. (iii) Emergency proclamations are NOT bills but resolutions under Articles 352, 356, 360; they follow a different procedure and are not classified as Money Bills. Any option including (iii) is therefore wrong.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The __________ Amendment of 1976 is often called the 'Mini Constitution' because of the wide-ranging changes it introduced.
questions.explanation: The 42nd Amendment of 1976 was one of the most extensive amendments — it added 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' to the Preamble, inserted Fundamental Duties (Part IVA), and made many other changes, earning it the nickname 'Mini Constitution'. The 38th Amendment dealt with a narrower emergency-related issue. The 44th Amendment (1978) reversed several of the 42nd's changes. The 52nd Amendment (1985) introduced the Anti-Defection Law.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The Attorney-General for India, the chief legal advisor to the Government of India, is appointed by:
options: Both Houses of Parliament by a special majority
questions.explanation: The Attorney-General is appointed by the President of India under Article 76. She/he holds office during the pleasure of the President. The Prime Minister does not appoint the AG — the PM (Council of Ministers) advises the President. The Chief Justice of India has no role in appointing the AG. Parliament does not appoint the AG; parliamentary approval is not required for the appointment.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the President of India:

(i) The President is the executive head of the country in whom the executive power of the Union is vested.
(ii) The President is elected directly by the people of India.
(iii) The President exercises powers on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.
(iv) The President can be removed only through impeachment for 'violation of the Constitution'.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — under Article 53, the executive power of the Union is vested in the President. (iii) is correct — Article 74(1) mandates that the President act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. (iv) is correct — impeachment under Article 61 is the only way to remove the President, for 'violation of the Constitution'. (ii) is INCORRECT — the President is elected INDIRECTLY by an Electoral College consisting of elected MPs and elected MLAs of States and UTs (Article 54), NOT directly by the people. Any option including (ii) is therefore wrong.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: Which of the following writs literally means 'we command' and is issued to direct a public authority to perform its official duty?
questions.explanation: 'Mandamus' is Latin for 'we command' — the writ orders a public official or lower court to perform a mandatory public duty. 'Habeas Corpus' means 'you may have the body' — used to prevent unlawful detention. 'Certiorari' means 'to be certified' — used to transfer a case to a higher court for review. 'Quo Warranto' means 'by what warrant/authority' — used to challenge a person's title to a public office.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The __________ of 1935 is one of the most important sources of the Indian Constitution and provided the model for the federal structure with a strong Centre.
questions.explanation: About two-thirds of the Indian Constitution's provisions are borrowed from the Government of India Act, 1935 — federal scheme, office of Governor, judiciary structure, emergency provisions and public service commissions. The 1919 Act introduced the diarchy in provinces — a smaller precursor. The 1947 Independence Act ended British paramountcy but did not itself supply structural blueprints. The Cabinet Mission Plan gave the framework for the Constituent Assembly but was not itself a source of provisions.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Article 32 has been described as the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.
Reason (R): Article 32 provides the right to move the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights through writs.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: (A) is correct — Dr. B.R. Ambedkar famously called Article 32 'the very heart and soul' of the Constitution. (R) is correct — Article 32 empowers a citizen to move the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights via the five writs. (R) explains (A) directly: it is the enforcement mechanism that makes rights meaningful. Option 2 wrongly denies the explanation. Options 3 and 4 wrongly deny (A) or (R).

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The Constitution of India originally provided how many Fundamental Rights?
questions.explanation: Originally there were 7 Fundamental Rights: Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, Right to Property, and Right to Constitutional Remedies. The 44th Amendment (1978) removed the Right to Property from Part III, leaving 6 Fundamental Rights currently. '5' is too low. '6' is the CURRENT number (after 1978), not the original. '8' is too high.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The office of the Lokpal at the Central level was created under the:
questions.explanation: The Lokpal is a central-level anti-corruption ombudsman established under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (enacted after the Anna Hazare movement of 2011). The RTI Act (2005) established the right to access government information, not the Lokpal. The Prevention of Corruption Act (1988) is a substantive criminal law on corruption but does not create the Lokpal. The Central Vigilance Commission Act (2003) governs the CVC, a separate body from the Lokpal.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText:
Match the following writs with their meaning/purpose:

Column I:
(a) Habeas Corpus
(b) Certiorari
(c) Prohibition
(d) Quo Warranto

Column II:
(i) Preventing an inferior court from proceeding with a case outside its jurisdiction
(ii) Ordering the production of an unlawfully detained person
(iii) Questioning by what authority a person holds a public office
(iv) Transferring a case from a lower court to a higher court for review

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: Habeas Corpus produces a detained person → (a)-(ii). Certiorari transfers a case from a lower to a higher court for review → (b)-(iv). Prohibition prevents a lower court from exceeding jurisdiction → (c)-(i). Quo Warranto tests the authority under which a public office is held → (d)-(iii). The distractor (a)-(iii) confuses Habeas Corpus with Quo Warranto. (a)-(iv) treats Habeas Corpus as Certiorari.

questions.subject: B
questions.questionText: The concept of 'Judicial Review' in the Indian Constitution is inspired mainly by:
options: The Constitution of the United Kingdom
The Constitution of the United States of America
questions.correctAnswer: The Constitution of the United States of America
questions.explanation: Judicial review — the power of the judiciary to strike down laws that violate the Constitution — is drawn primarily from the US Constitution (established by Marbury v. Madison, 1803). The UK operates under parliamentary sovereignty, where courts cannot strike down parliamentary law, so judicial review is limited there. Australia's judicial review draws from the same US model but was not the inspirational source for India. The Government of India Act, 1935 supplied structural details, not the doctrine of judicial review as such.
